title: Why the ringed nematic rods do not swim-then-divide: a rod moves fastest just after its birth by fission and slows with age (frame step 0.29-0.35 -> 0.13-0.25 px/frame), and slower growth lengthens the cycle but not the distance; without the chemostat the rods fuse into an active worm network with no persistent individuals
summary: Follow-up to 20261026T0300-c34-swimdivide. motionphase.py (labkit tracker) splits each long track's life into deciles: in four settings (zeta 0.8 and 1.0, phi_b -0.63 and -0.65) a daughter's mean step is highest in the first decile after fission (0.29-0.35 px/frame) and falls by a third to a factor 5 later, and its net displacement after 10/20/40 frames is 3.1/4.5-5.6/7.6-8.8 px in every setting. Lowering the bath level stretches a life to 100-180 frames without adding distance (median whole-life net 10-16 px), because late-life rods barely move (0.05-0.07 px/frame at phi_b -0.65). So part of the rods' motion is post-fission separation, and the rest is too slow and too unpersistent to reach 3 body lengths between divisions. Removing the chemostat (kr=0, seeds 0 and 1, T=1500) does not give a no-growth control: the volume fraction stays at 22% and the rods fuse into a dense active worm network (1264-1322 splits, 0 persistent; kr0/sheet.png), so the chemostat is what keeps the population dilute and individual.

finding.operator: extensile active stress on chemostatted CH rods
finding.control: 4 settings of activity and bath level; kr=0 (no chemostat) on 2 seeds
finding.result: first-decile step 0.29-0.35 px/frame vs 0.04-0.25 later; net 3.1 px after 10 frames in all settings; whole-life net 10-16 px; kr=0: 0 persistent splits, occupancy 0.22
